newsitem.title: USA: Lilly says Evista plans within 1997 budget.
newsitem.headline: Lilly says Evista plans within 1997 budget.

text.p: Eli Lilly and Co said Wednesday it hoped to meet 1997 Wall Street earnings expectations despite unexpected expenses of preparing to market Evista, its drug candidate for prevention of postmenopausal osteopororis.
The Indianapolis company earlier said the U.S. Food and Drug Administration had granted priority review status to Lilly's new drug application for Evista, whose generic name is raloxifene.
In effect, the FDA agreed to place the drug under a six-month review process rather than the standard 12-month review, Lilly said. The news helped lift shares 3-3/8 to 117 in afternoon trade.

"We'll probably see some expenses in the second half of the year related to Evista which otherwise might have been spread out partially into 1998," Lilly chief financial officer Charles Golden said Wednesday.

"We'll be needing to gear up activities for our sales forces and our advertising plans for Evista," he said, adding the expense "will provide a little bit of a challenge for us" in the second half of the year.
Golden said Lilly remained confident, nevertheless, of meeting Wall Street earnings projections for the year.
The First Call consensus analysts' estimate is an earnings per share of $3.21 for the year.
"I think at this point we are still very hopeful we can meet those expectations," he said.

Lilly, which matched the 1997 first quarter consensus estimate of $0.82, released its second quarter results Wednesday morning almost simultaneously with its announcement about the expedited FDA review for Evista.

Excluding one-time special charges that are not factored into First Call estimates, Lilly's net income for the second quarter was $417.2 million, or $0.76 a share -- matching the First Call consensus estimate.
Three special items reduced 1997 second quarter earnings by $3.90 a share, causing Lilly to report a quarterly loss of $1.73 billion, or $3.14 a share.
The biggest one-time item was a noncash charge against earnings of about $2.4 billion to write down the carrying value ot the company's PCS healthcare management business.
Lilly disclosed last month it would take the PCS write-off, conceding it paid too much when it acquired the pharmaceutical benifits management operation.
Golden on Wednesday said he was unable to provide PCS sales figures, but added it was making a profit although its margins were well below those seen for pharmaceuticals sales.
"Clearly thus far in 1997 (PCS) is making more than they did in 1996, (it's) not in a loss position," Golden said. "It is improving, but we have a long way to go."
